text.hook:
std::shared_ptr is two pointers and a control block.
Interviewers use it to test what you really know about ownership.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Handle, control block, object
2. What copy, move and reset cost
3. Two lifetimes: object vs control block
4. Type-erased deleters and when not to use make_shared
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Handle, control block, counts and deleters: what interviewers actually check.

slides.title: Three things, keep them apart

cards.label: Handle
cards.text: The `shared_ptr` object itself. Typically two pointers: stored pointer + control-block pointer.

cards.label: Control block
cards.text: Heap bookkeeping shared by all owners: counts, deleter, allocator.

slides.takeaway: Copying a `shared_ptr` copies the handle and adds one owner. It never copies the `T`.

slides.title: What lives inside it
rows: reaches 0: the block itself is freed
slides.takeaway: 16 bytes per handle is typical on 64-bit. The standard specifies no size.

slides.title: What each operation costs
rows: unchanged: free, but not an owner
slides.takeaway: Returning a `shared_ptr` by value does not bump the count: elision or implicit move.

slides.title: Object vs control block
steps: Strong count hits 0: the deleter runs **now**, even if `weak_ptr`s exist
The control block stays, so `weak_ptr`s can report "expired"
With `make_shared` the object lives **inside** the block: its storage waits too
Weak count hits 0: the block (and that storage) is freed

slides.title: The deleter is not part of the type

cards.label: Type-erased
cards.text: Different deleters, same `shared_ptr<T>` type: one vector can hold them all. `unique_ptr<T, D>` cannot.

cards.label: Remembers the real type
cards.text: `shared_ptr<Base> p = make_shared<Derived>();` runs `~Derived`, even with a non-virtual `~Base`.

cards.label: Except
cards.text: When the constructor only sees a `Base*`. Then it deletes through `Base*`: UB.

slides.takeaway: Still give polymorphic bases a virtual destructor: `unique_ptr` and `delete` have no safety net.

slides.title: When not to use it
items: You need a custom deleter: it has no deleter parameter
The constructor is private: compile error
Big object + long-lived `weak_ptr`s: memory stays allocated

items.myth: "Returning a `shared_ptr` by value makes the count 2 for a moment."
items.truth: Elision or move: no extra owner, no atomic.

items.myth: "The object is destroyed when both counts reach 0."
items.truth: Destroyed at strong 0. Only the control block waits for the weak count.

items.myth: "`shared_ptr<Base>` needs a virtual destructor to destroy a `Derived`."
items.truth: Not when built from `Derived*` or `make_shared<Derived>`. Declare one anyway.

items.myth: "Moving a `shared_ptr` costs the same as copying."

slides.hero:
Copy: one more owner.
Move: free.

A raw pointer:
owned exactly once.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Two shared_ptrs, one Session, one raw pointer.
Shared ownership, right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: It compiles without a single warning. That is exactly why interviewers like it.

slides.title:
Both handles own `raw`.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11 / glibc: `~Session` twice, then "free(): double free detected", abort
bullets: Every constructor that takes a raw pointer allocates a **new** control block.
Two blocks, each with count 1, each sure it is the only owner.
`observer` destroys the Session, then `owner` destroys freed memory again.
No global table maps addresses to blocks. A `shared_ptr` cannot find the other one.
slides.wrong: "`2 2`: they point to the same object"

slides.title: Copy the `shared_ptr`, not the raw pointer
slides.takeaway: A raw pointer becomes owned once. Every further owner is a copy of a `shared_ptr`.

text.hook:
fopen fails and returns nullptr.
The shared_ptr is empty, so the deleter never runs. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: This one surprises people who port code from unique_ptr to shared_ptr.

slides.title:
`missing.cfg` does not exist.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: UB in C. Observed (GCC 11 / glibc): SIGSEGV inside `fclose`
bullets: `shared_ptr(p, d)` with `p == nullptr` still allocates a control block: `use_count() == 1`.
When the last owner goes away, it calls `d(nullptr)`.
`unique_ptr` never calls its deleter on null. `shared_ptr` with a deleter does.
Piped to a file, `0 1` may vanish: the crash happens before the flush.
slides.wrong: "`0 0`: a null pointer has no owner"

slides.title: Filter null, or make the deleter null-safe
slides.tip: Or make the deleter null-safe: `[](FILE* f) { if (f) std::fclose(f); }`
slides.takeaway: Deleters passed to `shared_ptr` must handle null, or null must be filtered before wrapping.

text.hook:
"make_shared is faster" is what everyone says.
So we counted every call to operator new.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The counter is a replaced global operator new. Nothing else is hidden.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Measured, libstdc++ x86-64: `make_shared<int>` = one 24-byte block; `new int` form = 4 + 24 bytes
bullets: `make_shared`: object and control block in **one** allocation.
`shared_ptr(new int)`: `new int`, then a separate control block. Two calls.
One allocator call: less time, less per-allocation overhead.
Counts next to the object: often better locality. A bonus, not the reason.

slides.title: No naked `new`
bullets: C++17 sequences each argument fully, so that leak is gone. The idiom stays.
slides.takeaway: One allocation, no naked `new`. Skip it for custom deleters, private constructors, and big objects with long-lived `weak_ptr`s.

text.hook:
A linked list built from shared_ptr. No raw new, no delete, no cycles.
Smart pointers clean it up automatically. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: One million nodes, one reset. Linux, default stack size.

slides.title: What happens at `head.reset()`?
options: Leak: the nodes form a cycle

slides.verdict_sub: Linux, 8 MB default stack, GCC 11: segfault at -O0 and -O2. ASan: stack-overflow
bullets: Destroying a node destroys its `next`, which destroys the next node, and so on.
That is recursion: stack depth equals list length.
Measured: 40,000 nodes already crash at -O0. -O2 survives 80,000, not 1,000,000.
Same for `unique_ptr` lists and deep trees.
slides.wrong: "Smart pointers make destruction automatic". Automatic is recursive.

slides.title: Unlink the chain in a loop
bullets: If another owner still shares a middle node, the loop just drops our reference. That tail survives.
slides.takeaway: Recursive ownership means recursive destruction. Unlink long chains iteratively.
